summary: Registers media types for the RTP payload formats defined in the RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences. Some of these formats can also be used outside RTP, so having proper media type names helps wherever they appear. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Each sound or video format used in online meetings gets an official name tag. This note hands out those tags to the formats that were already defined.

questions: media types for rtp audio and video
rtp conference profile media type registration
what are rtp audio media types
subtitle: Gives the standard audio and video formats used in RTP conferences official media type names.

tldr.problem: RTP payload formats from the Audio/Video Profile (RFC 3551) needed registered media type names in the updated registration format, and some of them are useful outside RTP too.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC re-registers 19 audio subtypes and one video subtype under the audio and video media types, each with its parameters, security notes and contact details, without making technical changes.
tldr.outcome: Together with RFC 4855 it obsoletes RFC 3555, and it adds no new registrations.

today: RFC 4856 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 3555 together with RFC 4855, and the unit metadata shows no later RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What Is Being Registered
sections.content:
This document updates the media type registrations first made in RFC 3555 for the RTP payload formats defined in the RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences, RFC 3551. They become subtypes under the audio and video media types. Some of the formats may also be used for transfer modes other than RTP.

Payload formats that RFC 3551 references but that are defined in other RFCs are not included here. Their registrations are meant to be updated in revisions of the RFCs that define them.

The registrations follow the updated template and procedures in RFC 4288 and RFC 4855. The update makes no technical changes in the registrations.
sections.eli5: Meeting software needs agreed names for each kind of sound and picture. This note writes those names down in the official list using the newest form.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Because the media types registry is now more general, the RTP Payload Format section of the registry changes its wording: "MIME" is dropped from the registry title and table headings, leaving just "media type" and "subtype".

The reference for the listed types changes from RFC 3555 to this document. The listed types are audio/DVI4, G722, G723, G726-16, G726-24, G726-32, G726-40, G728, G729, G729D, G729E, GSM, GSM-EFR, L8, L16, LPC, PCMA, PCMU, VDVI and video/nv.

Some registrations from RFC 3555 are omitted here and stay valid until other RFCs update them. There are no new registrations.
sections.eli5: The big official list gets a small clean-up of its headings, and the old source note is swapped for this one. No new names are added.

sections.title: Audio Registrations and Their Parameters
sections.content:
For most audio payload formats, the RTP timestamp clock rate equals the sampling rate. Some formats work at one fixed sampling rate and others are adjustable. All audio formats here accept the optional parameters ptime (recommended length of time in milliseconds carried in a packet) and maxptime (the maximum), both defined in SDP (RFC 4566).

Several formats add their own parameters.

  • DVI4 requires rate; the typical value is 8000.
  • G723 has bitrate (5.3 or 6.3 kb/s) and annexa for voice activity detection.
  • G729 has annexb for voice activity detection.
  • L8, L16, PCMA and PCMU have channels, which defaults to 1.

For most of the entries, framing is described as framed binary data, the intended usage is COMMON, and the change controller is the IETF Audio/Video Transport working group, delegated from the IESG.
sections.eli5: Each sound style comes with a few settings, like how many seconds of sound go in each packet, or whether it is mono or stereo.

sections.title: The L16 Registration and Video
sections.content:
audio/L16 is the most detailed entry. It was first registered in RFC 2586 for transports other than RTP, and that registration is folded in here and extended for RTP. Its required rate parameter allows 8000, 11025, 16000, 22050, 24000, 32000, 44100 and 48000 samples per second for non-RTP transport; for RTP other values are allowed but those are RECOMMENDED.

Optional parameters include channels, emphasis (only emphasis=50-15, the preemphasis used with Compact Discs, is defined) and channel-order, which refers to RFC 3190. Unlike the other entries, L16 is defined for file-based transfer as well as RTP.

The only video entry is video/nv. For most video payload formats, including this one, the RTP timestamp clock rate is always 90000 Hz, so the rate parameter does not apply, and channel is not used.
sections.eli5: One sound style, L16, is plain uncompressed sound that can also be saved as a file. The one video style listed always counts time the same way, so it needs no extra settings.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3555
sections.content:
RFC 3555 is obsoleted by the combination of RFC 4855 and this document. RFC 4855 keeps the procedures and requirements, while the registrations themselves moved here.

The registrations were updated to the revised procedures in RFC 4288 and RFC 4855.

  • Transfer via RTP is now stated under restrictions on usage rather than encoding considerations.
  • The encoding considerations now warn that these types are framed binary data.
  • The change controller is named by current convention.
  • The channels parameter was clarified for L8, PCMA and PCMU.
  • A missing reference was corrected.
sections.eli5: The procedures and the list of names were split into two notes. The names were also tidied up, and a few instructions were made clearer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Users of these types face the security considerations of the RTP specification (RFC 3550). None of the types carries active content. The content is compressed audio or video to be decoded and presented, although several encodings are well suited to hiding data by steganography.

A denial-of-service threat exists for compressed encodings with uneven decoding cost, because an attacker can inject pathological datagrams. The RFC notes that none of the encodings here has an expansion factor greater than about 20. A receiver may also be overloaded simply by too many packets, and network-layer authentication MAY be used to drop unwanted sources, although authentication itself can be costly.

RTP over IP multicast gives a sender no knowledge of its receivers and no privacy, so security mechanisms for confidentiality and integrity are important. Since compression is applied end to end, encryption may be done after compression.
sections.eli5: These sound and video files cannot run hidden programs. The risks are people hiding secret messages in them, flooding a listener with too much data, or listening in, so conversations should be locked.
